transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Samir Gupta (Solutions Eng) ; Adam Rivera (CTO) ; Priya Nair (SRE) ; Leo Kim (ML Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on tail latency (p95/p99) behaviors for Helix's production workloads. Covered streaming vs non-streaming, batching windows, KV cache behavior (prefix+KV), quantization tradeoffs with int8/4-bit models, and network topology impacts for VPC/on-prem deployments. Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, Helix to send traces, schedule on-prem topology call.

Topics covered:
- p95 vs p99 characterization and what drives p99 spikes
- prefix/KV cache cold misses and healing
- batch sizing, batch windows and latency SLOs
- quantization: q4 vs q8/int8 effect on latency and tail behavior
- streaming vs non-streaming APIs and their effect on end-to-end p99
- network hops, TLS termination, and LB / NLB topology for VPC/on-prem
- suggested mitigations and monitoring hooks

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): all right everyone thanks for joining, um today Jordan and I will run through the tail latency deep dive. we have the traces you sent, priya, and some synthetic runs, and we want to align on root causes and next steps.
[00:18] Priya (Helix SRE): yeah thanks, uh quick note we had an alert last week — p99 spiked from ~450ms to over 1.2s for a few minutes during a customer peak. not sure if it's model side or infra.
[00:30] Jordan (Redwood SE): ok, good context. on our side we looked at the traces you uploaded, there are a couple of patterns: a lot of p99s correlate with KV cache misses and large request size, plus a small subset of network retries when requests hit a cross-region hop.
[00:45] Adam (Helix CTO): cross-region? we thought everything is in the same region for the private cluster. could be misrouting.
[00:50] Samir (Redwood): sometimes the control plane or LB ties to a standby in another AZ, or in on-prem setups an external NLB can route odd. also if you're using a CDN or API gateway it adds hops — that can blow up tail.
[01:05] Leo (Helix ML Eng): to add, our prompt sizes vary a lot; some requests have 2k tokens of context, which I assume is heavier on the KV cache. does Redwood do prefix caching?
[01:15] Jordan (Redwood SE): yes we do prefix and KV cache for transformer KV state. so small prompts typically get hit from cache, but long-context requests can force full model attention compute and cold KV writes. cold KV miss is one of the most common p99 drivers we see.
[01:30] Priya: can you explain the cold miss path? like what extra steps happen?
[01:35] Jordan: sure, when the request references tokens that aren't in the hot cache, the runtime needs to reconstruct KV segments, or fall back to a disk-backed blob (in dedicated/private setups) which adds serialization + disk IO. also you can get extra batching delay while waiting for KV to be loaded to the GPU, and that increases observed latency.
[01:50] Adam: disk IO? in our on-prem we use NVMe attached to the hosts, but maybe not optimized.
[01:55] Jordan: right, NVMe helps but there's still overhead. if the KV is sharded across nodes you get network fetches for the missing segments — that's a network hop that shows up in the p99.
[02:10] Maya: quick note on numbers: in our synthetic runs without KV misses we saw p95 ~220ms p99 ~360ms for the 7B-ish model; with occasional KV cold misses that p99 can jump >1s. these are illustrative.
[02:25] Leo: what about streaming vs non-streaming? We use streaming in some UX flows and non-streaming for batch. which has better tail characteristics?
[02:32] Jordan: good question. streaming generally reduces client-observed time-to-first-token because you get incremental results; that reduces perceived latency for interactive flows. however, tail behavior is nuanced: streaming requires smaller per-step latency but also depends on network packetization and HTTP/2 backpressure; non-streaming can hide some jitter because you only report when full response done, but the p99 can be affected by long decoding loops. we saw cases where streaming p99 is lower for first token but total completion p99 still spikes if backend stalls mid-sequence.
[02:58] Priya: so for our chat product, time-to-first-token is most important, but we also need tight p99 for full response for SLA. any config recommendations?
[03:05] Jordan: we typically suggest enabling streaming + a small initial token budget and aggressive KV prefetching. also shorten batch window for interactive endpoints to avoid adding batching latency. for throughput endpoints, increase batch windows and accept higher p95 to optimize per-token cost.
[03:20] Priya: what's a 'small' window?
[03:23] Jordan: depends on QPS. for sub-100 QPS interactive endpoints a 10–20ms window often works; for 200+ QPS you might do 5–10ms. but you need to balance throughput; shorter windows mean less batching and higher cost.
[03:35] Adam: you mentioned quantization earlier — does q4 or int8 change tail?
[03:40] Samir: yes, quantization reduces compute time but can add variance depending on kernel paths. for example q4 paths often use specialized kernels that are very fast for common sequence lengths, but for long sequences or when using grouped quantization you might end up in a fallback path that is slower, spiking p99. int8 (per-channel) tends to be more consistent but larger memory. we've seen q4 p95 improves a lot but q99 occasionally degrades if you hit a non-optimized kernel.
[04:05] Leo: so q4 gave us a 20% latency win median but we saw some outliers, that matches. any tuning?
[04:10] Jordan: we can recommend a hybrid policy: run q4 for most traffic, but for requests above a token threshold route to q8/int8 or a different shard that uses the more conservative kernel. Redwood's smart routing can do that automatically based on length or customer tier.
[04:25] Priya: routing — is that per-request? Concerned about complexity and cost.
[04:30] Maya: routing is policy-driven and can be per-request; your team can set thresholds. cost goes up a bit for routing but it reduces p99 for critical requests.
[04:38] Adam: about network hops and TLS termination — our security team insists TLS at the edge and internal TLS for service-to-service. does TLS add a lot to p99?
[04:46] Jordan: if TLS renegotiation or new TCP handshakes happen for a subset of requests, you'll see big spikes. Keep connections warm with keep-alives and connection pooling. also in on-prem, watch LBs that terminate TLS then reconnect — that doubles hops. If you can do TLS passthrough to the inference hosts you often shave off latency.
[05:05] Priya: we are using a managed ingress that terminates TLS then forwards. moving to passthrough might be tough.
[05:10] Samir: if passthrough isn't possible, at least ensure the LB is in the same AZ and supports long-lived connections and HTTP/2 for streaming. also check if the LB is doing header inspection or WAF — that can add ms per request and occasional spikes under certain payloads.
[05:25] Leo: curious about batching interactions with KV — does batching increase chance of KV miss latency being amplified?
[05:30] Jordan: yes, batching can amplify a single cold-KV miss because multiple requests wait in the batch for the slow one to load. that's why we have smart batching that can fast-path requests whose KV is hot and batch the cold ones into a separate queue, but it depends on your traffic pattern.
[05:45] Priya: is that feature available for dedicated/private?
[05:48] Jordan: yes, available across hosted, dedicated, and private. in private we can tune locality so KV shards stay on the same host for a given customer slice which reduces network fetches.
[05:58] Adam: for our on-prem setup, would you recommend pinning model and KV shards to specific hosts?
[06:03] Samir: yes, pinning reduces cross-node hops but reduces flexibility for autoscaling. tradeoff: lower p99 vs less dynamic capacity. if you have predictable load, pinning is beneficial.
[06:15] Priya: ok, what about monitoring hooks — what should we add to our SRE dashboards?
[06:20] Jordan: key signals: KV cache hit rate, KV fetch latency distribution, batch sizes over time, time-to-first-token, per-model p95/p99, network RTTs between service tiers, TLS handshake rates, and queue wait times. Also instrument GPU kernel fallback counts and quantization fallback counters.
[06:36] Leo: how do you measure KV hit? is that per-token or per-request?
[06:40] Jordan: we emit both. per-request hit fraction (e.g., % of prefix tokens served from hot KV) and per-token metrics. per-request is simpler for SLOs.
[06:48] Priya: are there known bug patterns that cause sudden p99 spikes we should look for?
[06:52] Jordan: yes: mis-sized batch windows after deploy, agents that suddenly increase prompt size, old model variants with non-optimized kernels, TLS termination misconfig after infra changes, and external connector timeouts (e.g., DB lookups in a middleware).
[07:05] Adam: do you have concrete mitigation playbooks?
[07:08] Samir: we do. quick mitigation: 1) temporarily reduce batch window for affected route, 2) enable streaming fallback for interactive, 3) route large requests to a dedicated shard, 4) warm KV before traffic peaks, 5) roll back to a previous model variant if new quantization caused regression. we can share the playbook doc.
[07:25] Priya: warm KV — how do we do that? pre-warm scripts?
[07:28] Jordan: yes, pre-warm by replaying representative prompts before peak traffic or use a background prober that touches likely prefixes. Redwood can provide a prober script that hits hot prefixes.
[07:38] Leo: about prober overhead — does prober itself add cost?
[07:41] Jordan: it's negligible if you schedule it off-peak and keep concurrency low; the idea is to amortize cost vs p99 risk.
[07:48] Priya: can you walk through a concrete trace example?
[07:50] Jordan: sure, sample trace we pulled: request enters LB [00:00:000], routed to host A [00:01:024], host checks KV hotset -> miss at [00:01:100], triggers remote fetch from host B [00:01:240] over internal network, host B loads NVMe page at [00:01:450], returns data [00:01:760], GPU loads KV and resumes decode, first token emitted at [00:02:100]. total end-to-end ~2300ms. the outlier was the NVMe read + cross-host RTT.
[08:28] Priya: wow that matches our 1.2s spike window. So cross-host NVMe read plus RTT is the culprit for those samples.
[08:35] Samir: that plus occasional TLS connection renegotiation — if the prober or client doesn't keep a persistent connection, you stack the extra 100–200ms.
[08:42] Adam: ok, for our on-prem PoC we want to try two things: pinning KV shards and enabling q8 fallback for long requests. can you help size the expected cost delta?
[08:52] Maya: yes, we can run a cost simulation. ballpark: using q4 everywhere reduces GPU hours by ~30% vs q8, but if we route 10% of requests to q8 fallback, cost delta is ~+3–5% and p99 improves significantly for the long requests. we'll send a spreadsheet with sample numbers.
[09:10] Priya: what about dedicated vs hosted — we are leaning private but need to know if private deployment increases tail risk.
[09:16] Samir: private gives you control over network topology, which if done well reduces tail risk. but it also shifts responsibility for networking — misconfig can introduce tail. Redwood's private deployment has an optional managed data plane where we help tune LB and KV locality.
[09:29] Leo: any known interactions with autoscaling? we use horizontal scale based on queue length.
[09:33] Jordan: autoscaling can increase p99 during scale events if new nodes start cold (KV misses). to mitigate: stagger scaling, use warm pools, or batch warm nodes before they accept traffic.
[09:44] Adam: does Redwood support warm pools in dedicated/private?
[09:47] Samir: yes, warm pool support and configuration for pre-warm size. we can propose settings based on your QPS and p99 targets.
[09:55] Priya: monitoring-wise, you'll provide traces and metrics; can you also include span-level traces for the sample outliers?
[10:00] Jordan: yes, we'll include distributed traces showing per-hop timings. they helped us identify the NVMe fetch in the sample.
[10:06] Adam: ok great. any infrastructure changes we should prioritize?
[10:09] Jordan: prioritize reducing cross-host KV fetches and ensuring LB pass-through or same-AZ forwarding. second, add prober + warm pool. third, implement routing policy for long requests to q8 fallback.
[10:21] Priya: one more: what about model compilation/kernel selection? we saw a deploy last month that regressed p99 even though median improved.
[10:28] Samir: kernel selection table can pick different kernels per sequence length and quantization. sometimes new kernels are faster median but have rare slow paths for edge cases. we recommend a canary rollout with p99 monitoring and an automatic rollback policy if p99 regresses. Redwood has rollout hooks for that.
[10:44] Leo: can we capture kernel fallback counts?
[10:46] Jordan: yes, that metric is included; we'll add it to the suggested dashboard.
[10:50] Adam: recap and next steps?
[10:52] Maya: recap — we identified cross-host NVMe reads + occasional TLS renegotiation as likely root causes for p99 spikes. Mitigations: pin KV shards or improve locality, enable q8 fallback for long requests, add prober + pre-warm, tune batch windows, and verify LB topology (prefer TLS passthrough).
[11:10] Maya: next steps — Maya to send benchmarking spreadsheet and sample traces with our annotations; Jordan to analyze missed KV patterns; Priya to export 14 days of prod LB logs; Samir to schedule on-prem topology review.
[11:22] Adam: thanks team, this was very helpful.
[11:25] Priya: thanks, we'll get the artifacts over.
[11:28] Maya: great, we'll follow up with proposed PoC plan and dates.
[11:32] End of meeting.
